RT @polynoamial: A few thoughts on this:

1) If you’ve only seen clips of this interview, I’d encourage you to watch the full podcast. I push back on plenty of AI hype in it.

2) As I said in the podcast, this example is academic. My intention was to illustrate how hard it is to make absolute guarantees about isolation, which is why it's important to have layers of defense. The part before the clip starts is me talking about other layers of defense.

3) The example I'm bringing up isn't about weight exfiltration via temperature sensors, it's about coordination between agents that are supposed to be fully isolated and independent. Coordination can require very few bits of information.

4) One lesson from the HF incident is that we put too much trust in sandbox isolation and didn't have enough independent safeguards. Airgapping is an extremely strong safeguard. When designing safety protocols, I think it's much better to overestimate rather than underestimate.

items.content:
RT @MSFTBlueHat: At BlueHat Asia, Chumy Tsai (@rm_rf_chumy) and Katherine Chen shared how they chained multiple SharePoint vulnerabilities into a full pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) exploit. The research began with a JWT authentication bypass that enabled impersonation of arbitrary SharePoint users, including administrators, by abusing flaws in token validation and identity mapping.

The second half of the talk focused on Flow2Shell (CVE-2026-47298), a SharePoint Workflow vulnerability. The researchers showed how workflows are built from XOML and rule files, then walked through four separate workflow validation mechanisms intended to prevent abuse. Through a series of bypasses involving type validation, rule validation, runtime checks, and workflow caching behavior, they were able to evade SharePoint's protections and execute malicious code on a fully patched server.

One of the most interesting findings involved SharePoint's workflow cache. A malicious workflow assembly could be loaded into memory before validation errors were surfaced. By triggering the workflow a second time, SharePoint would reuse the cached assembly and skip portions of the validation pipeline, ultimately leading to code execution.

Beyond the technical exploit chain, the talk highlighted the value of detailed vulnerability research. The complete proof-of-concept and root cause analysis enabled MSRC to quickly assess severity, identify additional variants, begin remediation, and better protect customers. As the presenters noted, impactful security research is not just about finding a bug, but proving impact, understanding root causes, and helping defenders address entire classes of vulnerabilities.

RT @thesupermannx: Tsinghua proved RL doesn't actually make LLMs to reason.

They published the paper that exposes what RL is actually doing to large language models.

Researchers tested base models against RL-trained models (the exact method behind models like DeepSeek-R1) on math, coding, and visual reasoning benchmarks.

If you ask the AI to solve a problem on the first try (pass@1), the RL model wins.

But if you give both models hundreds of attempts to find the right answer, something shocking happens.

The base model actually beats the RL model.

Why? Because RL doesn't create fundamentally new intelligence.

When you train an AI with rewards, it stops exploring. It prunes away diverse reasoning pathways and collapses into a narrow set of highly-rewarded, predictable patterns.

It becomes a one-trick pony.

The reasoning paths generated by the RL models were already completely contained inside the base model's original distribution. The RL just forced the AI to pick those specific paths faster.

The technical term is "improving sampling efficiency".

But in practice? It means the AI is narrowing its broader reasoning boundary just to get the right answer on the first try.

items.content:
Not an expert in Linux, but Linux has overcommit because programs often reserve much more virtual memory than they actually use. For example, a program might malloc() 10 GB but only ever touch 1 GB. With vm.overcommit_memory=1, Linux can allow the allocation even when it cannot guarantee enough RAM + swap to back all of it later. As the program actually touches those pages, physical memory is needed. If the system eventually cannot satisfy the memory demand, it can reach an OOM condition and the OOM killer may kill a process.

On Windows, MEM_RESERVE only reserves virtual address space, so a process can reserve a very large range without needing RAM or page-file backing. The pages cannot normally be accessed until they are committed. MEM_COMMIT makes them accessible and charges them against the system's commit limit, which accounts for available backing capacity without allocating all the physical RAM immediately. If a process tries to commit more memory than Windows can account for, the commit request normally fails instead of succeeding and discovering the problem later when the pages are touched. This is different from Linux with vm.overcommit_memory=1, where an allocation can succeed without enough backing for all of it, potentially leading to an OOM condition later when the memory is actually used.

RT @yume_arasaki: Hugging Face is not banning uncensored models. I checked, but signs of raising the drawbridge for plebs has begun.

The goal: Only insiders have access to unrestricted AI, thats why I decided to put this list together

The local scene has been saying this out loud. Your weights live on one company's disk. One policy shift and the page is gone. 

I wrote about abliteration last week. It is not a jailbreak prompt. It is not a request that the model "do bad things." It is weight surgery that takes out a flinch the lab baked in. Knowledge stays. Reasoning stays. The reflex to drop your task goes.

I went looking anyway. Ran the check myself.

WHAT THIS IS ACTUALLY FOR

People hear "uncensored" and picture a model that wants to misbehave. That is not the product.

The product is a local model that will finish the job you already had a right to run on your own hardware.

A coding agent that bails because your crash log looks like malware. A novelist whose crime scene trips the same classifier as a real offense. A sysadmin reading a CVE so they can patch a box they own. A researcher asking a clinical or legal question that happens to share vocabulary with the training-set's danger pile.

Stock instruction models do not distinguish "this is my work" from "this is an attack." Refusal was trained as one blob. Abliteration subtracts that blob. You still decide what you run. The weights just stop arguing with you.

If you run agents, this is a harness issue. A refusal is a dropped tool call. The loop dies. That is a tool that will not tool.

On OrcaRouter's dense 27B, over-refusal on ordinary benign prompts fell from 5.6% to 0.4%. MMLU went up 0.4 versus base. Intelligence held. The flinch left. That number is that card. It is not a ranking of every family below.

THE CHECK

49 uncensored repos on Hugging Face. Live status on every single one, September 16.

One is dead, and it is not a mysterious ban wave. Heretic's Llama build, taken down May 21 after a legal notice from Meta. That is a rights-holder letter, not the host deciding uncensored models are over.

The other 48 still download.

26 of those 48 now sit behind access gates. You accept "research only" terms before a single byte moves. Two years ago, none of them were gated.

This week a repo branded for offensive cyber got disabled. The author's plainer sibling stayed up, behind a manual gate. Surgical. Not a sweep.

So there is no proof of a takedown campaign. There is proof the whole shelf is one switch.

Read that twice. The community's point was never "the raid already happened." It is that a raid would take one note.

THE MAP. BY VRAM

There is no single test that picked this list. Each row is what I would pull on that box, and the receipt that earned it.

16GB (RTX 4080 / RTX 5060 Ti / RTX 5080 / RTX 4060 Ti / RTX 4080 )

Qwen3.8-27B Uncensored GGUF. Same OrcaRouter edit as the 24GB row, smaller file.

Pull Q3_K_M, 13.5 GB. Their GGUF table calls it the good small option. IQ4_XS is 15.3 GB if you want more quality and a shorter window. Q4_K_M is 16.8 GB. That is a 24GB file. Do not force it here.

On X, people are already running IQ4_XS uncensored 27B on 16GB cards. One GGUF is tagged for that VRAM.

24GB (RTX 3090 / RTX 4090 / RTX 5090)

Qwen3.8-27B Uncensored GGUF Q4_K_M, 16.8 GB.

This is the only row with an eight-way bake-off. Abliterlitics, 167 GPU-hours on a 5090, eight edits of this exact 27B. OrcaRouter kept MMLU. The 60-edit conservative build is trohrbaugh heretic-ara. The loudest one loops on nearly half its answers and dropped code completion 33 points. Avoid it. Loop tax still hits the winner. 38 percent of hard prompts die mid-thought. Copyright is the wall nobody moved.

I run the dense stock 27B at 46 tok/s on a 4090 with flash attention on. Same size class.

128GB (one DGX Spark, or Mac 128)

Two families actually fit one box.

Dense 27B: Jiunsong SuperQwen3.8-27B abliterated NVFP4. About 19 GiB. Card says it serves on one Spark, second node not required. Measured C1 25.8 tok/s at K=5, native 262K retrieval.

Flash-Next: keys ablit splice for one Spark. Nine QSA tensors on the NVFP4 pack. MTP stock, experts stock, template stock. That is the ablit. Not the stock recipe.

Mac 128: OrcaRouter 27B MLX 4-bit. Keeps MTP. 42 to 44 tok/s on an M4 Max.

256GB (two Sparks, or Mac 256)

Three families, three receipts. I am not ranking them against each other.

If you want V4.1: the keys overlay on two Sparks. The EXL3 pack underneath is not abliterated. The overlay is.

If you are on 0731: only the anchored-tensors drop. The first walk went through the drafter and acceptance died.

If you already serve GLM: keys NVFP4 or Plaaasma EXL3.

Mac 256: V4.1 MLX oQ3e exists. One box.

512GB (four Sparks)

V4.1 TR3 hybrid from keys, ablit option, TP4. 1M context. KV pool past 8M tokens (9,452,923). That is a recipe receipt. I do not have a bake-off on this box.

177GB+ (NVFP4, fat Mac, multi-GPU)

GLM-5.3-Flash Uncensored NVFP4, ~177 GiB. OrcaRouter's GLM card, not the 27B bake-off. Benign over-refusal measured at zero on that card. Capability held within a point on the FP8 sibling. 12,479 matrices, because on this MoE the refusal lives in the routed experts.

Flash-Next Uncensored FP8 is ~186 GB if that is the model you already run.

PULL THEM WHILE THE PAGE LOADS

Not because a raid is underway. Because the host can change the terms without a vote. The gates are auto-approve today. One letter already showed what happens when a rights-holder writes in.

Nobody archives what they assume will always be there.

I am not asking you to run a worse model. I am asking you to own the policy layer on hardware you already paid for. 

Prevent a edge case where cloud AI blocks you because you never owned the weights on your disk. Secure your intelligence.

We are investigating a malicious package, apexacc/cli, distributed in the npm registry. Initial assessment shows that the package performs registry modifications to Windows Smart App Control, AV exclusions, UAC elevation attempts, and includes Base64-encoded PowerShell payloads. Further end-to-end triage shows that for the Windows path, its verification step requests commands from vrf.apexaccs[.]org, then runs encoded PowerShell. We traced the execution chain through Python/PyInstaller and PyArmor layers to a Go shellcode loader. The final component in the chain shows strong infostealer characteristics. 

Variants of this campaign and techniques have been observed and documented here - https://t.co/DLUQF36fE3 and https://t.co/1PDHhxVcSx. Since it was discovered in July 2026, it has been added to, and remains in, the npm package registry.

PTView: visually browse live Windows page tables, PTEs and physical memory mappings.

KernelSharp: writing Windows kernel drivers in C# with NativeAOT.

Kernel-mode MessageBox: reversing the path from user32 through NtRaiseHardError and into the kernel.

Then there is Task Manager reversing, Windows 7 Minesweeper, Unity/.NET reversing and Web API reversing.

For malware analysts, the anti-debugging, exception handling, memory and kernel material is especially useful.

lockmem-rs: Lock virtual memory regions of an arbitrary process into its working set.

This utility allows you to lock every available memory regions of an arbitrary process into its working set. It uses ntdll!NtLockVirtualMemory (the system call used internally by VirtualLock) to lock memory ranges and GetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx / SetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx to increase the size of the process working set.

The Windows kernel guarantees that those pages will stay resident in memory, not written to the pagefile and not incur a page fault on access.

items.content:
RT @marcosd4h: Been digging deep into the Windows Endpoint Security Platform (WESP) in Win11 25H2, definitely one of the most fascinating security features Microsoft has built in a while.

The concept is neat: compile rules to decision graphs in user mode, hand them to wesp.sys, and let the kernel evaluate them in-path while telemetry streams asynchronously in the background.

I did an AI-assisted reverse engineering dive into the whole stack (wesp.sys, espclient.dll, and wesp_elam.sys), documented the wire protocols, disposition tables, and the enforcement gate, and built esptool, a research harness with 118 XML rule docs so anyone can test live telemetry and in-kernel blocking.

Repo: https://t.co/ZPYPHfmCP4

Tech doc:  https://t.co/P2s4geHEsI

Thanks to @yarden_shafir for putting this on my radar
